title: 2 Kings 5:15–27
context: 2 Kings 5:15–27 records what follows the healing. Naaman returns to Elisha and confesses that there is no God in all the earth but in Israel. Elisha refuses his gift. Naaman asks for two mules’ load of earth so that he can worship the LORD alone, and he asks pardon in advance for bowing beside his master in the house of Rimmon. Elisha answers, "Go in peace." Gehazi, Elisha’s servant, runs after Naaman, lies to obtain silver and clothing, and lies again to Elisha, who announces that Naaman’s leprosy will cling to Gehazi and his offspring. Both traditions read Naaman’s confession as genuine Gentile faith, and they read Gehazi’s punishment as narrative judgment on greed and deceit. Interpreters in each tradition discuss what "Go in peace" implies about the request concerning Rimmon, and the text itself does not settle that question.

verses.text: He returned to the man of God, he and all his company, and came, and stood before him; and he said, “See now, I know that there is no God in all the earth, but in Israel. Now therefore, please take a gift from your servant.”
verses.arminianNotes: Naaman returns to Elisha and declares that there is no God in all the earth but in Israel, and he offers a gift. Arminians see a genuine confession of faith from a Gentile who has experienced God’s power and now acknowledges the LORD alone.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the confession as the true purpose of the healing (5:8). Both traditions read Naaman’s words as real faith, shared ground between them, and see his offer of a gift as gratitude, though not yet a full understanding of grace.

verses.text: But he said, “As the LORD lives, before whom I stand, I will receive none.” He urged him to take it; but he refused.
verses.arminianNotes: Elisha swears, "As the LORD lives, before whom I stand, I will receive none," and refuses even when urged. Arminian readers see Elisha making clear that God’s gift is free and that the prophet is not a hired healer.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and see the refusal as protecting the truth that grace cannot be purchased. Both traditions note the contrast with Gehazi in 5:20–24 and read Elisha’s refusal as faithfulness to the God he serves.

verses.text: Naaman said, “If not, then, please let two mules’ load of earth be given to your servant; for your servant will from now on offer neither burnt offering nor sacrifice to other gods, but to the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: Naaman asks for two mules’ load of earth, saying he will now offer sacrifices only to the LORD. Arminians see a new believer expressing his commitment in the way he understands, connecting the worship of the LORD with the land of Israel.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note that ancient people often linked a god with a land. Both traditions read the request as sincere devotion to the LORD alone, and both avoid turning the earth itself into a point of disagreement or a theology of sacred soil.

verses.text: In this thing may the LORD pardon your servant: when my master goes into the house of Rimmon to worship there, and he leans on my hand, and I bow myself in the house of Rimmon. When I bow myself in the house of Rimmon, may the LORD pardon your servant in this thing.”
verses.arminianNotes: Naaman asks the LORD to pardon him when his master leans on his arm and he bows in the house of Rimmon. Arminian readers see an honest conscience aware of a conflict between his new faith and his duties at court, and they note that he asks for pardon rather than permission to worship Rimmon.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree that the request shows a tender conscience. Interpreters in both traditions differ on whether the bowing is a civil duty or a compromise that is simply left to God. Both agree the text records the request without explaining how God regarded it.

verses.text: He said to him, “Go in peace.” So he departed from him a little way.
verses.arminianNotes: Elisha says, "Go in peace," and Naaman leaves. Arminians read the words as a blessing that sends Naaman home in God’s peace, without giving a detailed ruling on every question he raised.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree that the words are a blessing and note that the text does not say whether Elisha approved the request about Rimmon. Both traditions treat the verse as shared ground and avoid building a general rule from it.

verses.text: But Gehazi the servant of Elisha the man of God, said, “Behold, my master has spared this Naaman the Syrian, in not receiving at his hands that which he brought. As the LORD lives, I will run after him, and take something from him.”
verses.arminianNotes: Gehazi says his master has let Naaman go without taking his gift, and he swears by the LORD to run after him and take something. Arminian readers see greed taking hold of a servant who had seen God’s power, and the oath by the LORD makes his sin more serious.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and note the irony that Gehazi uses the same oath as Elisha in 5:16 for the opposite purpose. Both traditions read the verse as the beginning of a narrative judgment on greed.

verses.text: So Gehazi followed after Naaman. When Naaman saw one running after him, he came down from the chariot to meet him, and said, “Is all well?”
verses.arminianNotes: Gehazi follows Naaman, who comes down from his chariot and asks whether all is well. Arminians see Naaman’s humility and courtesy toward the prophet’s servant, a change from his earlier pride.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the contrast between the Gentile’s new humility and the Israelite servant’s greed. Both traditions read the verse as heightening the shame of Gehazi’s deception.

verses.text: He said, “All is well. My master has sent me, saying, ‘Behold, even now two young men of the sons of the prophets have come to me from the hill country of Ephraim. Please give them a talent of silver and two changes of clothing.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: Gehazi lies that Elisha has sent him to ask for a talent of silver and two changes of clothing for two young prophets. Arminian readers see deliberate deceit that misuses Elisha’s name and threatens to make the free gift of God look like something paid for.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and see the lie as damaging the witness Elisha had just given. Both traditions read Gehazi’s story as a warning about using religious service for personal gain.

verses.text: Naaman said, “Be pleased to take two talents.” He urged him, and bound two talents of silver in two bags, with two changes of clothing, and laid them on two of his servants; and they carried them before him.
verses.arminianNotes: Naaman insists that he take two talents and has two servants carry the silver and clothing. Arminians see Naaman’s generosity, which Gehazi exploits for his own benefit.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note that Naaman’s gratitude is sincere even though Gehazi’s request is false. Both traditions read the verse as showing how deception takes advantage of the generosity of others.

verses.text: When he came to the hill, he took them from their hand, and stored them in the house. Then he let the men go, and they departed.
verses.arminianNotes: At the hill Gehazi takes the goods, stores them in the house, and sends the men away. Arminian readers see him hiding his gain, which shows that he knew what he was doing was wrong.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and see the concealment as part of the sin. Both traditions read the verse as preparing for the confrontation in which Elisha reveals what Gehazi tried to hide.

verses.text: But he went in, and stood before his master. Elisha said to him, “Where did you come from, Gehazi?” He said, “Your servant went nowhere.”
verses.arminianNotes: Gehazi goes in to his master, and when Elisha asks where he has been, he says he went nowhere. Arminians see one lie leading to another, as Gehazi adds deceiving his master to his earlier sin.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the question as giving Gehazi an opportunity to confess, which he refuses. Both traditions read the verse as showing how sin hardens when it is not acknowledged.

verses.text: He said to him, “Didn’t my heart go with you when the man turned from his chariot to meet you? Is it a time to receive money, and to receive garments, and olive groves and vineyards, and sheep and cattle, and male servants and female servants?
verses.arminianNotes: Elisha says his heart went with Gehazi and asks whether this is a time to receive money, garments, olive groves, vineyards, flocks, and servants. Arminian readers see the prophet’s insight exposing the sin and naming the possessions Gehazi may have been dreaming of.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree. The list goes beyond what Gehazi actually took, and interpreters read it as describing what he hoped to buy. Both traditions see the rebuke as showing that his greed damaged God’s witness to Naaman.

verses.text: Therefore the leprosy of Naaman will cling to you and to your offspring forever.” He went out from his presence a leper, as white as snow.
verses.arminianNotes: Elisha declares that Naaman’s leprosy will cling to Gehazi and his offspring forever, and he leaves as white as snow. Arminians read the punishment as just judgment fitting the sin, since Gehazi took Naaman’s silver and receives his disease.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the reversal: the Gentile goes home clean, and the Israelite servant becomes unclean. The word "offspring" can also be translated "seed." Both traditions read the judgment as narrative, warning against greed and deceit in God’s service.
